title: Collaborative Planning Meetings
author: Hart, Nick
summary: Hart outlines how collaborative planning meetings can improve teaching quality when focused on substance: subject content sequencing, pedagogy, misconceptions, task design, and adaptation. He warns against tokenistic sharing and emphasizes planning at least two weeks ahead to allow time for team feedback. Leadership teams must strategically choose which subjects to examine in depth based on data and teacher needs. Hart provides mental models for both planning for other teachers (clarity, slide notes, plenty of practice, advance sharing) and preparing to teach lessons planned by others (seeking clarification, providing feedback, rehearsing explanations).
points: Quality of teaching is the biggest difference to outcomes; school leadership shapes the organization conditions that influence teaching quality most.
Collaborative planning must focus on substance: content, pedagogy, misconceptions, task design, adaptation—not superficial tokenistic sharing.
Planning must occur at least two weeks ahead so team feedback can actually improve plans before implementation; Friday meetings create weekend work.
Leadership teams should strategically focus deep collaboration on subjects with lower achievement data or weaker team subject knowledge.
Teachers preparing to teach shared plans owe children their preparation: clarification, feedback, checking misconceptions, rehearsing explanations.
quotes: It is the quality of teaching that makes the biggest difference to outcomes for children and school leadership has a significant effect on features of the school organisation which positively influences the quality of teaching and learning.
By choosing to collaborate in depth on some subjects, it is inevitable that other subjects will not be looked at together which makes it even more important to have clarity of expectations.

There are versions of planning meetings that might not be as useful as others. For example, superficial tokenistic sharing of planning: This is what we're doing in maths next week. Any questions? If this is how planning meetings run, there needn't be a meeting.

Any meeting of time-poor teachers needs to be purposeful. The best use of time is to focus on the substance of subject content, pedagogy, misconceptions, task design and adaptation.” Archived from Mr. Nick Hart on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
